nodes.label: API customer
nodes.summary: An application or user sending chat or completion requests and reading the streamed tokens.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.summary: Authenticates, applies per-customer token-based limits and quotas, validates the request and streams tokens back (server-sent events). Standard platform design; no vendor publishes theirs.
nodes.details: Rate-limit algorithms and overload behaviour: see note 02. The vLLM paper only describes a serving system behind an API, not a gateway.

nodes.label: Request Router
nodes.summary: Chooses a replica by current load, and for long shared prefixes can prefer a replica that already holds that prefix's KV cache. Cross-replica prefix routing is our design extension.

nodes.label: vLLM-style engine replica
nodes.summary: One engine process per GPU group: a centralized scheduler with a KV cache manager coordinates GPU workers that run the model.

nodes.label: Scheduler
nodes.summary: Decides every iteration which requests run: first-come-first-served, finished requests leave and new ones join between iterations, and the latest requests are preempted when GPU memory runs out.
nodes.details: Iteration-level scheduling is Orca's mechanism; vLLM schedules first-come-first-serve and preempts the latest requests, with swap-to-CPU or recomputation.

nodes.label: KV Cache Manager
nodes.summary: Splits each request's KV cache into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens), keeps a block table from logical to physical blocks, shares prompt blocks with copy-on-write, and hands out and frees blocks.

nodes.label: GPU Workers (model executor)
nodes.summary: Run one model iteration for the scheduled batch using the paged attention kernel. For large models, tensor model parallelism (Megatron-style SPMD) spreads the model across GPUs.

nodes.label: Model weights store
nodes.summary: Where model weights are loaded from when a replica starts. Loading is slow, which is why scaling is hard. Weight size is parameters times bytes (about 26 GB for a 13B model in FP16).
nodes.details: The 26 GB figure for a 13B model is in the vLLM paper; the store itself and its cold-start behaviour are our design reasoning.

nodes.label: Usage metering
nodes.summary: Counts input and output tokens per customer for billing and quotas.

nodes.label: Metrics and alerts
nodes.summary: TTFT, TPOT, queue time, GPU memory, preemptions and error rates per replica. Feeds the autoscaler and on-call.
nodes.details: TTFT and TPOT are defined in the DistServe paper; the monitoring setup is our design.

nodes.label: Autoscaler
nodes.summary: Adds or removes replicas based on queue depth and latency targets, with a warm floor because loading weights is slow and GPUs are scarce.

nodes.label: Alternative: separate prefill and decode GPUs
nodes.summary: DistServe assigns prefill and decoding to different GPUs to remove interference and tune parallelism per phase, at the price of moving the KV cache between them (about 1.13 GB for a 512-token OPT-66B request; it places both phases on one machine to use NVLink when cross-node bandwidth is low). It reports 7.4x more requests or 12.6x tighter SLO. Sarathi-Serve's chunked prefill is the competing approach on shared GPUs.

steps.caption: The request arrives with an API key; the gateway checks the key and the customer's token limits.
The admitted request is passed to the router.
The router picks a replica by load (and, in our design, by prefix) and hands the request to its scheduler.
The scheduler asks the KV cache manager for blocks for the prompt; more blocks are allocated as tokens are generated.
Each iteration the scheduler runs the batch on the GPU workers; the prompt is processed in parallel, then tokens come one per iteration.
Tokens are streamed back through the gateway as they are produced.
Input and output tokens are counted for the customer.
A running request needs a new block and none is free.
The scheduler preempts the latest request, evicting all of its blocks (all or nothing). Its state is swapped to CPU memory or recomputed later. The earliest requests keep running.
The remaining batch continues; the preempted request resumes when blocks are free again.
Queue depth and time to first token rise on the replicas.
The autoscaler sees the signals cross its thresholds.
Each new replica must first load the model weights, which is slow, so the extra capacity arrives late. A warm floor and scaling ahead of known peaks reduce the gap (our design reasoning).
